title: Gregory's return and the bond of love
english: Oration 24. On the holy hieromartyr Cyprian, on the speaker's return from the country one day after the commemoration. Cyprian almost slipped away from us—what a loss! And you allowed it, you who admire the man more than anyone and honor him year after year with feasts and public celebrations. Cyprian—the one whom even those who forget everything else must remember among the things that matter, if indeed the best are most to be remembered, and those whose memory is at once holy and profitable.

But let us pay the debt with interest, if we can show ourselves to have such resources—if indeed we are not altogether lacking and poor. And if we are very poor, I know he will forgive us both the delay and the poverty, since the man is in every way great-souled and a philosopher. Only let us give thanks that he did not escape us. Let us give thanks, for it is right.

We must begin this way: we have returned to you at a good moment, by God's good measures—God who orders and directs all things in weight and measure—from stillness to speech, from love of the martyr to the martyrs, from bodily rest to spiritual feasting.

We were longing for you, my children, and you were longing for us in equal measure—I am convinced of it. You see a father's right feeling: I speak of my own, and I testify to yours. We were separated from one another just long enough to recognize and test our longing through absence, as painters do with their panels, and now we have come together again.

How great a spark of memory even a brief companionship of friends is—for those whose character is loving and who imitate God's love for humanity! How could we not, as disciples of Christ, who emptied himself for us to the point of taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7) and gathered us, strangers to the heavenly things, to himself—how could we not hold fast to one another and cling to one another, and keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Ephesians 4:3), which is the mystery, or rather the sum, of the law and the prophets?

This, then, is the first and foremost benefit: that we ran to one another as quickly as possible and embraced. For zeal does not tolerate delay, and a whole lifetime is a single day to those worn out with longing.

The second benefit, and the greatest, is that we did not come running after the feast was over, nor were we left behind from the initiation into the martyrs and the delight and refreshment that comes to us from it.

For I confess that in everything else I am more sluggish than anyone. I have shaken off every desire since I enlisted with Christ, and I choose none of the things that others find delightful and eagerly pursue: not wealth that is dragged along the ground and overturned, not the pleasures of the belly and the satiety that is the father of insolence, not soft flowing clothing, not the brilliance and charms of precious stones, not music that bewitches the ear, not fragrance that makes one effeminate, not the applause of crowds and theaters that drives men mad—all of which we long ago surrendered to those who want them—not any of the offspring of that first taste of ours, through which we were ruined. Indeed, I condemn the great foolishness of those who allow themselves to be mastered by these things, corrupting the nobility of the soul with pettiness about them, and clinging to things that are passing as if they were permanent.

But for that other thing I have an insatiable hunger and I cling to it, and I approve of this passion in myself. I delight in the honors of the martyrs, and I rejoice in the blood of the athletes. Others have the contests and the victory; mine are the crowns.
orientation: Gregory of Nazianzus is opening his panegyric for the hieromartyr Cyprian, explaining that he has just returned from the countryside one day after the annual commemoration and is now addressing the congregation.

title: All martyrs must be honored, Cyprian most of all
english: This is how eagerly I seize their good order in advance, and how fully I make their triumphs my own! Every martyr deserves our festival, and for every martyr we should readily open tongue and ear and mind, speaking eagerly about them and listening, and counting everything less than their contest.

That is how it truly stands. We have many guides toward what is better, and many schools of training in virtue: speech, the Law, the prophets, the apostles, and the sufferings of Christ himself, the first martyr, who went up upon the cross and gathered me with him, so that he might nail my sin to it (Colossians 2:14), and triumph over the serpent (Colossians 2:15), and sanctify the wood, and conquer pleasure, and save Adam, and call back the fallen image. With guides so many and so great, the martyrs still teach us no less. They are reasonable sacrifices, perfect victims, acceptable offerings, proclamations of the truth, public shaming of falsehood, the fulfillment of the Law, at least of the Law understood spiritually, the overthrow of error, the driving out of evil, a flood against sin, and the cleansing of the world.

But you, Cyprian, mean more to me than any other, in both deed and name — more than the other martyrs, although martyrs feel no envy toward martyrs. Your virtue has conquered me in a special way, and I am lifted by your memory, and I become almost inspired with joy, and in a sense I stand beside your witness, and I share in your contest, and I pass over wholly to you. Perhaps this comes from our kinship in words, in which you surpassed other men as much as rational beings surpass an irrational nature — for somehow, I know not how, affection steals in among those joined by anything at all, no less in other pursuits than in closeness of blood. Perhaps it comes from the sudden and astonishing character of your conversion, which is beyond speech and example. For the sun is sweet after the cloud that had hidden it, and spring is sweeter still because it comes after the gloom of winter, and a smiling calm is lovelier, and the sea spread flat and playing against the shore, after the winds have ceased and the waves have ceased laboring.

This Cyprian, gentlemen — so that those who know may find remembrance sweeter, and those who do not know may learn the finest of our stories and the common pride of Christians — this is that man, once the great name of Carthage and now of the whole world, conspicuous for wealth, distinguished for power, and notable for birth, if sharing and presiding in the senate is the greatest proof of nobility. He was the flower of youth, the image of nature, and a power in words, both in philosophy and in every other kind of education, and in whatever branch of them you choose. In each field, people admired variety more than mastery, or rather they admired his distinction in each field more than his breadth of learning in all. To put it more plainly, he surpassed some by variety, others by mastery, and still others by both, but he surpassed all men in all things.

His own discourses witness to his eloquence, the many brilliant works he laid down on our behalf, since he transferred his education, by the love for mankind of God, who makes all things and refashions them toward the better, and he bowed irrationality before the Word. From here on I do not know how to use speech or what to become: how to avoid spinning out a long speech, wholly out of season, if I recall everything in Cyprian, and how to avoid cheating those present of the greatest things by what I leave unsaid.
orientation: Gregory addresses his congregation to praise all martyrs as teachers and then singles out Cyprian for his learning and sudden conversion.

title: Cyprian's evil past and the virgin who resisted him
english: To hold a middle course between the occasion and the longing of my hearers, this seems to me the right thing to do: to leave the rest to those who know it, and to instruct those who do not, if there are any, so that both sides receive the same benefit, those who teach Cyprian's deeds and those who learn them, since even remembering the man is sanctification, and my speech is the greatest encouragement to virtue. But I shall touch briefly on one or two of his deeds, and only those which no one could pass over even if he wished.

I shall mention his former life, and what road brought him salvation, and what his calling was, and his conversion toward the better. It would be utterly base and small-minded to suppose that the athlete is insulted by remembering his baser days. For otherwise even Paul the great would not deserve our praise, Matthew the tax collector would be ranked among the worst, and so would Cyprian himself. Paul remembered his own former persecutions, and the conversion of his zeal, so that by the contrast he might glorify his benefactor all the more. Matthew adds the Tax Collector to his own name in numbering the disciples, as if it were some other honorable distinction. And Cyprian himself holds his own former wickedness up to public shame in a long account, so that even his confession may bear fruit for God, and he may become for many who turn from wickedness a road toward better hope.

Consider, then, what that wickedness was, and how great its magnitude. He who later became a disciple of Christ had been a servant of demons. He who became a great champion of the truth had been a most bitter persecutor. He who afterward was mightiest in both for Christians had troubled our way in both word and deed, through his power in both. And add to these the evil of sorcery, the most well known thing about him. Add too bodily lust, more terrible still, which can madden even men wise in all else and forces them to think basely, snatching reason away like an unruly colt.

But my story now reaches its very head. Let no one look to Cyprian's beginnings and set his heart on pleasures; let him learn self-control from Cyprian's end. There was a virgin of noble and modest birth. Listen, virgins, and rejoice with her, and even more all you married women who are self-controlled and love self-control, for this story adorns you both alike. And the virgin was very beautiful in appearance. Let the divine David sing of her with us, saying, "All the glory of the king's daughter is within" (Psalm 45:13), a true bride of Christ, beauty set apart, a living statue, an inviolable offering, an untrodden sanctuary, kept for Christ alone. Let Solomon too add his verse, "a garden locked, a spring sealed" (Song of Songs 4:12).

Great Cyprian was caught by her, though she was in all things secure and modest, and I do not know from where or how. For greedy eyes touch even what must not be touched, the readiest of organs and the most insatiable. Cyprian was not only caught, but he also made an attempt on her. What folly, if Cyprian hoped to plunder her, and what shamelessness rather in the one who both dares such things and persuades men to dare them. That devil from the beginning slipped into paradise against the first creature, and he stands in the midst of angels to demand Job, and at the last he dares against the Master himself, who will destroy him and put him to death, and he brings trial upon the One who cannot be tried, since he saw God's visible presence as a second Adam, as if he would wrestle even him to the ground.
orientation: Gregory pauses his praise of Cyprian's eloquence to tell new hearers about Cyprian's earlier life as a worshipper of demons and persecutor and about the noble virgin whose resistance led toward his conversion.

title: The virgin conquers and the demon turns on Cyprian
english: He did not know that in rushing at humanity he would run straight into divinity. So what wonder if through Cyprian too he makes trial of a holy soul and an untouched body? Cyprian made the attempt, and for his procurer he took no practiced old woman skilled in such business, but one of the demons that love bodies and love pleasure. For the rebellious powers are swift to serve such ends, and envious, since they seek many companions in their fall. And the pay for this procuring was sacrifices and drink offerings, and bonding through blood and fat smoke. Such had to be the wages for those who grant such favors.

But as soon as she sensed the evil and recognized the plot — for pure souls shaped toward God are quicker to scent the one at work, however crafty and varied his attack — what does she do, and what art does she turn back against the craftsman of evil? Giving up all other hope, she flees to God, and against this hateful lust she makes her own bridegroom her protector, the one who rescued Susanna and saved Thecla, the one from cruel elders and the other from a tyrannical suitor and a still more tyrannical mother. Who is he? Christ, who rebukes spirits, and lifts the baptized, and walks upon the sea, and consigns a legion of spirits to the deep. He rescues from the pit the righteous man thrown to the lions as prey, who overcame the beasts by the stretching out of his hands (Daniel 6:22). He rescues the runaway prophet swallowed by the great fish, who kept his faith even in its belly (Jonah 1:17). He saves the young Assyrians in the flame, cooling the fire with an angel and joining a fourth to the three (Daniel 3:25).

Crying aloud these deeds and still more, and begging Mary the Virgin to aid a virgin in danger, she puts forward the remedy of fasting and sleeping on the ground. At once she withers her beauty as a traitor, to draw the fuel away from the flame and burn up the tinder of the passions. At once she wins over God through faith and through humility. For among all things God is served by nothing as by hardship willingly borne, and His love for mankind is answered with tears.

I know you long for what comes next in the story. For you are anxious for the virgin, and no less for her lover, lest desire end in ruin for them both. But take heart. For desire becomes the occasion of faith. And the lover, while wooing a virgin for himself, is himself wooed by Christ. And the flame of lust is quenched, while the flame of truth is kindled.

How, and in what way? Here for me is the sweetest part of the story. The virgin wins, the demon is defeated. The tempter comes to her lover and reports his defeat. He is treated with scorn. He resents the scorn and takes vengeance on the man who scorned him. And what is the vengeance? He settles and dwells inside Cyprian himself, his former worshiper, so that evil may be driven out by evil, and frenzy become the cure of frenzy. From the virgin he is driven back, as a siege-engine from a strong and noble wall, fleeing before word and prayer. But he grapples with the one who sent him — O the wonder! — turned back against the one who threw him, and throttling him like a second Saul.
What then does the foolish lover do, a self-controlled man now seized? He seeks release from the evil, and he finds it. For everyone under pressure becomes resourceful.
orientation: Gregory is recounting how Cyprian sent a demon to seduce the Christian virgin and how she resisted by fleeing to God.

title: Cyprian burns his books and becomes bishop
english: What was his release? He fled to the virgin's God, as Saul once fled to David's lyre and the striking of its strings. He came to her Shepherd. He was cleansed, and as the wound cured his desire, so faith in Christ cured him of the evil spirit. His desire was changed. For a long time he was disbelieved and turned away. The thing seemed beyond belief and wonder, that Cyprian should ever be numbered among Christians, even if all other men were. Yet he was changed, and the proof of his conversion was plain to see. He laid his books of sorcery out in public. He triumphed over the weakness of that evil hoard. He proclaimed its folly. He raised a bright flame from the books themselves, and consumed in fire that long deception, which had offered no defense against a single flame of fleshly desire. He broke with the demons and was made kin to God. O the grace! How great a thing it is that with evil desire and an evil spirit he finds God. He became a holy sheep of the holy flock and, as I heard from one man, even a sacristan, having begged earnestly to practice lowliness as his philosophy, to cleanse his former arrogance. Then he became a shepherd, and among shepherds the strongest and most approved. For he presided not only over the Church of the Carthaginians, nor over Africa, made famous through him and because of him to this day, but over all the west, and nearly over the east itself as well, and over the southern and northern lands, as far as his wonder had reached. In this way Cyprian became ours.

These are the works of the God of signs and wonders. These are His works, who brought Joseph down into Egypt, sold cheap through the spite of his brothers, and tested him through a woman, and glorified him through the giving of grain, and made him wise through dreams, so that he should be trusted on foreign soil, and honored by Pharaoh, and become father of many myriads, for whose sake Egypt was afflicted, the sea was parted, bread was rained down, the sun was stayed, and the promised land was given as an inheritance. For wisdom knows how to lay the foundations of great deeds from far off, and to order opposites by opposites, so that it is wondered at all the more. Even these deeds of Cyprian are enough to make up the measure of the most perfect praise.

But what remains is so much and of such a kind that, even if none of the things already spoken belonged to him for praise, what follows alone would suffice for him to surpass all. To cut short what lies between, there was his contempt for money, his destruction of pride, his disciplining of the body and purity to match his former impulses, his philosophy in dress, his bearing in audiences, both lofty and humane, standing equally far from meanness and arrogance, his lyings on the ground, his watchings, in which, though a late learner in such things, he far surpassed those who came before, his zeal for words, by which he trained every character, and cleansed ignorance of doctrines, and adorned the lives of men, and brought back to its ancient state the Godhead of the princely and royal Trinity, which was being divided, and by some even being confounded together, while he remained within the bounds of pious union and joint reckoning. To gather all this into brief compass, since it is boundless, I shall end my speech with the ending of his life.

Decius raged against us and devised every form of punishment, and some of the terrible things were already present, and some were still to come. He made it an equal contest both to seize Christians and to surpass the persecutors before him, or rather, either to seize all Christians or to seize and produce Cyprian alone.
orientation: Gregory is still telling how Cyprian was converted and then made bishop before the persecution under Decius.

title: Cyprian makes martyrs by letter from exile
english: For the more Decius recognized how far Cyprian excelled in devotion and renown, the more conspicuous and brilliant he judged his own victory would be if he mastered him. In the one course he would master only Christians, but in the other he would master philosophy itself and eloquence. To cut out the tongue first, and then to carry off voiceless and speechless those who leaned on it, seemed to him the finest strategy. He reasoned in this unjust and impious way, yet not entirely without calculation for his own desire and enterprise. And events proved it.

For after Cyprian had shaken off every attack and trial with courage and nobility, like a sea cliff shaking off the rush of waves, at last Decius condemned him to exile. The noble man did not cling to his own concerns, nor did he love being kept safe. He did not reckon disgrace as safety for the body so much as quiet, and watching others face danger in the crisis, as danger to the soul, with no trainer to train them and embolden them for the contest. For speech added to courage is no small help to those who strip for the stadium of virtue.

So he was absent in body but present in spirit, and he contended alongside those in the contest. He could no longer help with his tongue, but he helps with his pen. How? He becomes an anointer beyond the border, writing letters of encouragement and composing works in defense of devotion, and almost single-handedly he makes more martyrs through his letters than all those present in person made among the sufferers of that time. He persuades those who risk their lives for what is good to put neither homeland nor family nor wealth nor power nor any other earthly thing before the truth and the prizes of virtue laid up above. This, he says, is the finest business, to buy the kingdom of heaven with a little blood and to receive eternal glory in exchange for passing goods.

For there is one homeland for the exalted, the Jerusalem of the mind, not the lands here divided by narrow boundaries and changing their many inhabitants. There is one splendor of birth, to guard the image and to become like the archetype as far as is possible for prisoners of the flesh who can receive only a slight outflow of the good. There is one power, might against the evil one and a soul unconsumed and undefeated in the contests for devotion, when vice contends against virtue and world against world, the dissolving against the standing, and the bitter judge of the contest against noble champions, and Beliar is arrayed against Christ. For these reasons he urged them to despise swords and to count fire as cold, to reckon the wildest beasts as tame and to regard the highest luxury as hunger, and to run past the tears and laments and wailings of their kin as lures of the evil one and hindrances on the divine journey. These responses belong to courageous and noble souls and to self-controlled reason. And the example stood close at hand in the man himself who spoke and wrote these things, who counted all things as refuse in order to gain Christ (Philippians 3:8).

With this mind Cyprian armed many for the contest by his words and made them athletes. And what payment does he receive for this work? How rich and generous it is! He becomes a martyr after all those he sent ahead, beheaded by the sword, and upon his many tortures he sets this crown.
orientation: Gregory shows how Decius exiled Cyprian to silence him, and how Cyprian still strengthened the persecuted by letters until his beheading.

title: Cyprian's hidden body revealed for the common good
english: So Cyprian is brought to Christ; so he is converted toward Christ—Cyprian, who was great in impiety and greater still in godliness, the great persecutor and crown-winner, a man no less admirable for his conversion than for his virtue. For it is not so great a thing to preserve the pattern of goodness as it is to make godliness something new. The one belongs to habit, the other to sound judgment; the one is found in many people, but of the other there are few examples.

But what about this other wonder of his? Let us linger a little longer on the account, so that we may give a gift to the athlete. Such was the man's way of life, and such was the manner of his contest. And when he ended his life—if it is right to say this, rather than to call what happened to him a departure to God, or a fulfillment of longing, or a release from bonds, or a separation from a burden—something worthy of what had gone before was worked as a wonder even here. The name of Cyprian was on everyone's lips, and not only among Christians but also among those arrayed against us, for what is good is equally revered by all. But his body was hidden, and the treasure was kept by a certain woman fervent in piety, and this for a long time. I do not know whether God was honoring her love for Him, and for that reason she was holding fast to the martyr, or whether He was training our longing, in case we could not bear to suffer loss and be deprived of the relics of the saints.

But the God of martyrs did not allow the good of all to become the private possession of one person, nor did He permit the common benefit to be diminished by His favor toward her. He made the body public through a revelation, entrusting this honor to a certain woman among the worthy, so that women too might be sanctified. Just as women first gave birth to Christ and then announced Him to the disciples after His resurrection from the dead, so now one woman revealed Cyprian and another handed over the common benefit. This is the last of his good deeds. So the man who deserved not to be hidden comes into the open, and he is not permitted to make a philosophy of his own theft, since he is greater and higher than the honors paid to bodies.

These things, then, are what we have to offer, and I do not know that more needs to be said. For even if we stretched out a long speech, we could not say anything worthy of what belongs to him and of what each person has understood about the man. And we have gone through these things only so far as to discharge the honor owed to him. The rest you must add from yourselves, so that you too may bring something to the martyr: the overthrow of demons, the destruction of diseases, the foreknowledge of what is to come. All these things even the dust of Cyprian can do together with faith, as those who have experienced it know—those who have passed the wonder down to us and will hand it on to the time to come.

But rather, bring forward things greater than these, the things that befit those who honor him genuinely: emptying of the body, ascent of the soul, flight from evil, increase in virtue. Let virgins bring their freedom from the flesh, women their good order in virtue rather than in the body, young men their courage against the passions, elders their sound counsel, those in power their respect for law, those in command their gentleness, those skilled in words their reasonableness. And let me say something of what belongs to us: let priests bring their guidance in the mysteries, the laity their obedience, those in mourning their consolation, those in prosperity their fear, the rich their generosity, the poor their gratitude. Let all bring their battle array against the evil and bitter persecutor, so that he may not strike when he appears, may not shoot his arrows while hidden, may not wage war as darkness, may not play as an angel of light and steal people away to the pit of destruction.
orientation: Gregory has just described Cyprian's beheading and now turns to the wonder of how his hidden body was later revealed by God.

title: The eternal reward and final doxology
english: It is a terrible thing to be captured through the eyes, wounded through speech, lured through the ear, set ablaze through seething anger, dragged down through taste, softened through touch, and to use the weapons of salvation as weapons of death. We ought rather to fence ourselves with the shield of faith and stand against the schemes of the Evil One, and after conquering with Christ and contending with the martyrs, to hear that great voice: “Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom promised to you” (Matthew 25:34), where all who rejoice have their dwelling, and they dance a dance that cannot be dissolved; where there is the sound of those keeping festival and the voice of gladness, and a more perfect and purer illumination of the Godhead, whose enjoyment now comes in riddles and shadows.

Cyprian rejoices to be honored by these things more than by all others put together. These are what he pursued as his philosophy in his life while he was present, and what he now urges upon you all through my voice, though he is absent. Do not dishonor that voice in any way, if you care at all for his steadfast endurance and his contests on behalf of the truth, and for me who commends these things to you.

These are the firstfruits of my words to you, O divine and holy head. This is my gift of honor to you, both for your words and for your contest: not an Olympic wild olive, not Delphic apples, those playthings, not Isthmian pine, not the celery of Nemea, with which unfortunate youths were honored, but a word, the thing most fitting of all for those who serve the Word. And if it is worthy of your contests and your words, it is the gift of the Word.

May you watch over us from above with favor, and guide our word and our life, and shepherd this holy flock, or shepherd it together with us, directing all things as far as possible toward what is best, and driving away the heavy wolves, the hunters of syllables and of expressions. And may you grant us a more perfect and brighter illumination of the Holy Trinity, of which you are now an attendant, whom we worship, whom we glorify, in whose city we live as fellow-citizens, worshiping the Father in the Son, the Son in the Holy Spirit. May we also stand beside it in the end, sincere and without offense, and may we perfectly share in it, perfected ones, in Christ himself our Lord, to whom be all glory, honor, and might forever and ever. Amen.
orientation: Gregory is closing the oration, contrasting the dangers of the senses with the eternal joy promised to those who conquer with Christ, and he offers his speech as a gift to Cyprian before a final prayer and doxology.
